title: Auditing Structured Randomness for Quantum Error Correction under a Bounded Cloud Fault Model
authors: Ziqing Guo, Anthony Lawrence, Renyu Wang, Randy Kuang, Ziwen Pan
abstract: Cloud quantum processors compile submitted quantum error correction circuits and may colocate them with untrusted workloads. A fixed public encoder gives a fault-injection adversary a reusable target. Per-run reseeding changes the physical-to-logical fault map. Exact Haar-random encoders have exponential circuit cost. Efficient random ensembles provide average-moment guarantees and leave worst-case accepted corruption uncharacterized. We define accepted logical disturbance, an acceptance-weighted measure of harmful logical action in accepted results, and derive its exact Haar expectation. We evaluate a polynomial-cost seeded Clifford encoder family using dense linear algebra and gate-level stabilizer simulation against faults chosen before or after the encoder is known. Reseeding reduces mean accepted logical disturbance from 0.150 for faults chosen after learning each encoder to 0.020 for one fault chosen before it is known. The 86.7% reduction results from rejection. The fixed distance-three \([[5,1,3]]\) code corrects every tested weight-one Pauli, while 18.5% of sampled encoders in the selected ensemble satisfy exact quantum error correction. The measured reduction quantifies the integrity gain from reseeding and separates postselected detection from exact correction under explicit fault and attacker-knowledge models.
summary: This paper develops a rigorous audit framework to measure the integrity of QEC circuits running on untrusted cloud quantum hardware. By defining 'accepted logical disturbance,' the authors quantify how much corruption slips through the system despite error correction. They demonstrate that implementing per-run reseeding significantly boosts the system's resilience against sophisticated fault-injecting adversaries.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical issue of auditing the integrity of Quantum Error Correction (QEC) circuits executed on untrusted cloud quantum processors susceptible to fault injection.
main_result: Reseeding the encoder significantly reduces the mean accepted logical disturbance from 0.150 to 0.020, quantifying a major integrity gain against sophisticated adversaries.
method: The authors define 'accepted logical disturbance' as an acceptance-weighted measure and derive its exact Haar expectation, evaluating this using a polynomial-cost seeded Clifford encoder family.
model_or_system: The model involves QEC encoding ($V_s$) on cloud quantum processors, where an adversary injects Pauli faults ($Q$) into the physical-to-logical fault map. The analysis uses both seed-aware and seed-blind attacker models.
key_observables: Accepted logical disturbance, which quantifies harmful logical action in accepted results; the reduction factor between seed-aware and seed-blind fault models.
important_parameters: Fault weight ($t$), code parameters (e.g., $[[5,1,3]]$ code), and the ratio of disturbance reduction ($\Delta_{blind}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the fault set $\mathcal{E}_t$ is restricted to Pauli strings and relies on the mathematical properties of Haar-random unitaries for expectation calculations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the integrity audit process, classifying outcomes as rejected, harmlessly accepted, or accepted with logical corruption. Table 1 compares the proposed audit against prior methods.
paper_structure: The paper first defines the security metric (accepted logical disturbance) and derives its Haar expectation. It then evaluates this metric using a seeded Clifford encoder family under two distinct attacker knowledge models (seed-aware vs. seed-blind), culminating in quantitative results demonstrating the benefit of reseeding.
why_interesting: While focused on QEC, the rigorous mathematical framework for quantifying 'accepted corruption' and separating detection from actual error correction provides a generalizable robustness auditing tool applicable to any complex, fault-prone quantum computation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Integrity audit. A client samples a fresh executable encoder Vs and submits the encoded state to a remote processor exposed to a bounded fault E. The provider observes the compiled seed; a co-tenant that commits before compilation is seed-blind. Inverse decoding and the ancilla syndrome test separate rejection, harmless acceptance, and accepted logical corruption.

Figure 2. Dense results for k = 1 over 200 seeds per condition. (a) Closed-form Haar expectations (lines) and measured seed means (markers) for acceptance and accepted disturbance. (b) Fraction of n = 8 encoders that correct every tested single- qubit fault, plotted against the median source-level two-qubit instruction count. Connected points are HSE depths; the diamond is uniform Clifford. Crosses mark median worst- fault disturbance above 0.5; open circles mark values below it. Bars show 95% bootstrap intervals in (a) and Wilson intervals in (b).

Figure 3. HSE ablation and attacker knowledge. Left: paired ablation at (n,k,d) = (8,1,12) over 200 seeds. (a) Change in worst-fault disturbance relative to the full HSE; squares show means and shading the central 90%. (b) Fraction of seeds safe against every tested fault; labels give mean two-qubit instruction counts. Right: (c) held-out scores at n = 8 for seed-aware, seed-blind, and uniformly random fault selection. Bars show 95% intervals.

Figure 4. Gate-level HSE results over 20 seeds per condition. (a) Fraction of single-qubit Pauli faults that cause an accepted logical change in ideal circuits. (b) Fraction of all noisy shots that are both accepted and corrupted under gate-local depolarization with (p1, p2) = (10−3,10−2). Points show seed means and bars show 95% bootstrap intervals. Neither panel includes idle or leakage noise.
